$comment: Rows a reviewer who teaches to this curriculum set after reading the official text beside the derived crosswalk; they win over the derived rows. Written by scripts/curricula/apply-review.js from the review files; `why` is the reviewer's reason.

K:scene-search.why: Finding every look-alike in a busy scene is visual discrimination; the child neither names shapes nor describes positions, so it is a readiness step for K.G.A.1, not the standard itself.

K:order-by-size.why: Ordering three to five objects by length or height is 1.MD.A.1 (order three objects by length); K.MD.A.2 only compares two objects, so seriation goes beyond it.

K:patterns.why: The K.OA domain is addition and subtraction and says nothing about patterns; the only Common Core standard on shape patterns that follow a rule is 4.OA.C.5, for which this is readiness.

K:one-to-one.why: Matching each object with a partner object pairs objects with objects, not with number names; it is the readiness step for K.CC.B.4.a and for the matching strategy of K.CC.C.6.

K:count-how-many.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units (an American K-1 teacher and math coach): saying the last number as how many there are is K.CC.B.4.b, which the rows left out. The two rows from the point's own codes stay.

was.why: Writing the numeral for a counted set is also K.CC.A.3 (represent a number of objects with a written numeral), which was missing.

K:colour-by-number.why: Colour-by-number is numeral recognition; the child writes no numerals and represents no count, so it only prepares K.CC.A.3.

K:count-forward-missing.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units: the pages have the child WRITE the missing numbers to 20, which is K.CC.A.3 (write numbers from 0 to 20) beside K.CC.A.2.

K:dot-to-dot-sequence.why: Joining dots from 1 practises the count sequence by ones (K.CC.A.1); only the sheets that start at 11 count forward from a given number (K.CC.A.2).

K:before-after-back.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units: the number after is one more and the number before is one less, K.CC.B.4.c ('each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger'). K.CC.A.2 (count forward from a given number) stays.

K:ordinal-position.none: Ordinal numbers (1st to 10th) are not in the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics at any grade.
K:ordinal-position.why: K.CC.B.4 is about cardinality (counting tells how many); ordinal position is a different idea and is not a readiness step toward it.

K:tally-marks.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units: tally marks are not named in Kindergarten; they first serve the Grade 1 data work (1.MD.C.4, organize and represent data). The counting itself stays K.CC.B.5.

K:combine-groups.why: Putting two groups together and counting all is adding within 10 with objects or drawings (K.OA.A.2), which was missing.

K:take-away.why: Crossing out and counting what is left is subtracting within 10 with drawings (K.OA.A.2), which was missing.

K:count-on.why: The skill itself names 1.OA.C.5 as the standard it leads to; that readiness row was missing.

K:number-bonds-k.why: Finding the partner that makes ten is K.OA.A.4, which was missing.

K:mirror-image.why: Nothing in the Kindergarten Geometry domain concerns reflection; recognising a mirror image is readiness for line symmetry, 4.G.A.3 (the standard the grade 2 symmetry points already use).

K:fact-fluency-colour-code.why: K.OA.A.5 covers fluency within 5 only; the within-10 sheets are 1.OA.C.6 and fluency within 20 is 2.OA.B.2. [pages-review en.review.json, 2.OA.B.2 prepares] The only lesson is a Grade 1 lesson on facts within 10; the code asks for fluency within 20.

1:write-the-equation.why: 1.OA.A.1 is solving word problems with unknowns in all positions; writing the equation for a picture where all three numbers are visible is K.OA.A.1 and only prepares 1.OA.A.1.

1:patterns-missing.why: Mapped to nothing while K:patterns was mapped; completing a repeating pattern is readiness for 4.OA.C.5 (shape patterns that follow a rule), the same as the Kindergarten point.

1:sort-three-groups.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units: sorting into three categories and asking which has the most and the fewest is 1.MD.C.4 (data with up to three categories), which the rows left out; K.MD.B.3 is the Kindergarten step it reviews. L.K.5.a (sort words into categories) is a language standard and does not belong on a math point.

1:ordinal-numbers.none: Ordinal numbers and ordinal words are not in the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics at any grade.
1:ordinal-numbers.why: The Counting and Cardinality domain has no ordinal content, and grade 1 work cannot be readiness for a Kindergarten domain.

1:number-line-placement.why: Locating whole numbers on a number line with equally spaced points is the first part of 2.MD.B.6, which was missing (the grade 2 number-line point already uses it).

1:odd-even-pairs.why: Deciding odd or even by pairing objects and checking for a leftover is exactly what 2.OA.C.3 asks; it was marked readiness only because of the grade, while the same skill in K is marked teaches.

1:add-three-addends.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units: the page adds three groups of pictures and has no word problem, so it is not 1.OA.A.2 (word problems with three addends); adding an easy pair first is the associative property, 1.OA.B.3. It prepares 1.OA.A.2.

1:fact-families.why: Found by the reviewer of the Grade 2 unit Fact Strategies Within 20 (an American Grade 2 teacher, 2026-11-13): thinking of the addition fact to subtract within 20 is a mental strategy of 2.OA.B.2; the Grade 1 lessons prepare it, the Grade 2 lesson teaches it. The three rows of the earlier reading stay.

was.why: Found by the reviewer of the first units (an American K-1 teacher): the two addition facts of a fact family are the commutative property, 1.OA.B.3 'Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract', which the derived rows left out. The two rows from the point's own codes stay.

1:bar-model.why: Nothing in the skill reaches within 100 or two-step problems; the part-part-whole and comparison bar is the drawing of 1.OA.A.1 and a readiness step for 2.OA.A.1.

1:fluency-within-20.why: Adding and subtracting within 20 mentally and fluently is the wording of 2.OA.B.2, which was missing. [pages-review en.review.json, 2.OA.B.2 prepares] The only lesson is a Grade 1 lesson on facts within 10; the code asks for fluency within 20.

1:check-answers.why: 2.NBT.B.9 asks children to explain why strategies work using place value; marking worked sums right or wrong is not that, it is the true/false judgment of 1.OA.D.7. [pages-review en.review.json, 1.OA.D.7 extends] The only lesson is a Grade 3 lesson in a within-1,000 unit, and true-or-false equations are not practiced.

1:bar-graphs.why: Bar graphs are named first in 2.MD.D.10 (draw a single-unit-scale bar graph for a data set); colouring a bar graph from counts is that standard, which was missing.

1:tens-and-ones.why: 2.NBT.A.3 is about numbers to 1000; expanded form of two-digit numbers is a readiness step for it (as the number-words point is already marked).

1:skip-counting.why: 1.NBT.A.1 is counting by ones to 120 and says nothing about skip-counting; counting by tens is K.CC.A.1 and by fives and tens is 2.NBT.A.2.

1:open-number-line.why: Showing sums and differences within 100 on a number line is 2.MD.B.6, which was missing; nothing in the skill reaches within 1000, so 2.NBT.B.7 is prepared, not taught.

1:bonds-to-100.why: 1.NBT.C.6 is limited to multiples of 10 in the range 10-90; partners of 100 (100 minus 30) go beyond that range, so the relation is extends.

2:hundreds-chart-moves.why: 2.NBT.B.8 is about numbers 100-900, which a hundreds chart never reaches (prepares only); moving by tens and ones to find a number or count the jumps is the place-value strategy of 2.NBT.B.5.

2:expanded-form-digit-value.why: The value of a digit in a three-digit number is 2.NBT.A.1, which was missing.

2:solids-in-real-life.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units: matching named solids to objects is Kindergarten work (K.G.A.1, K.G.A.2). 2.G.A.1 names only the cube among solids and asks for drawing shapes from attributes, which the page does not do.

was.why: Matching a real object to the solid it is shaped like is K.G.A.1 (describe objects in the environment using names of shapes), the most exact standard, which was missing.

2:read-jugs.why: 3.MD.A.2 names liters only; milliliters first appear in 4.MD.A.1 (relative sizes of l and ml), which reading a jug to 1000 and 2000 ml prepares.

2:choose-units.why: 2.MD.A.1 is about choosing and using measuring tools, not units; judging whether centimeters or meters, inches or feet fit is the unit sense of 2.MD.A.3 (estimate lengths in those units).

2:equal-groups-times.why: Writing the multiplication sentence for equal groups is 3.OA.A.1 (interpret a product as groups of objects), which was missing; 2.OA.C.4 stops at repeated addition.

2:arrays.why: Matching an array to a multiplication is 3.OA.A.1, which was missing; 2.OA.C.4 only asks for a sum of equal addends. Rows and Columns of Squares (year design 2026-11-14) has the child cut a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count them: 2.G.A.2.

2:share-and-group.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units: sharing a pile into equal groups is 3.OA.A.2. It does not prepare 2.OA.C.4 (arrays as repeated addition), which the same Grade 2 unit teaches before it.

2:symmetry-line.why: Deciding whether a line is a mirror line and picking the symmetric picture is what 4.G.A.3 asks (recognise a line of symmetry, identify line-symmetric figures); it was marked readiness only because of the grade.

2:symmetry-complete.why: Drawing the missing half of a figure is not a readiness step: it goes beyond 4.G.A.3, which only asks to recognise and draw lines of symmetry.

2:tangram-orientation.none: The page compares the orientation of finished tangram figures with a shadow; nothing is composed, so 1.G.A.2 (compose shapes) does not describe it, and Common Core names no standard for orientation in these grades.
2:tangram-orientation.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units.

3:estimate-by-rounding.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units: the page rounds two numbers and adds them (3.NBT.A.1). 3.OA.D.8 is two-step word problems whose answers are checked by estimation; the page has no word problem, so it only prepares that standard.

was.why: Rounding the addends to the nearest 10 or 100 is 3.NBT.A.1, which was missing.

3:thermometer.why: Found by the reviewer of the English math units: reading a thermometer does not lead to 3.MD.B.3 (scaled picture and bar graphs). It prepares the weather data of NGSS 3-ESS2-1 only.

was.why: Reading a temperature off a scale is not yet representing weather data in tables and graphs (3-ESS2-1); in mathematics the nearest standard is reading a scaled graph, 3.MD.B.3. Both are prepared, neither is taught (the mathematics reviewer's note, applied by the builder's own audit).

3:mult-div-relationship.why: Finding an unknown factor in an equation relating three numbers is 3.OA.A.4, which was missing.

3:input-output.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): a table that follows a printed rule is named outright at 4.OA.C.5 (a pattern that follows a given rule); 3.OA.D.9 stays.

3:balance-equations.why: The meaning of the equal sign is 1.OA.D.7; 3.OA.A.4 covers equations relating three numbers, so an equation with an operation on both sides goes beyond it. [pages-review en.review.json, 1.OA.D.7 extends] The only lesson is a Grade 3 lesson in a within-1,000 unit, and true-or-false equations are not practiced.

3:time-12-24.none: 24-hour time is not in the Common Core; 2.MD.C.7 and 3.MD.A.1 use the 12-hour clock with a.m. and p.m. only.
3:time-12-24.why: 2.MD.C.7 is telling time to five minutes with a.m. and p.m.; converting between 12-hour and 24-hour notation is not what it asks.

3:equivalent-fractions.why: The parent standard also covers comparing fractions; recognising equivalent fractions as the same amount is exactly components 3.NF.A.3.a and 3.NF.A.3.b. Whole Numbers as Fractions (year design 2026-11-14) writes whole numbers as fractions and finds fractions that are equal to whole numbers (3 = 3/1, 6/1 = 6, 4/4 = 1): 3.NF.A.3.c.

3:fraction-of-set.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): 3.NF.A.1 is a fraction of one whole cut into equal parts; one third of 12 is equal sharing (3.OA.A.2) in Grade 3 and first appears as a fraction of a set at 4.NF.B.4.

K:pre-writing-strokes.why: Pre-writing strokes are the readiness step for printing letters; the handwriting standard was missing.

K:beginning-sounds.why: Sorting pictures by beginning sound is also isolating the initial phoneme; RF.K.2.d was missing.

K:sound-position.why: Found by the reviewer of the first units: the pages of this point do not stop at hearing. They ask the child to WRITE the letter a picture ends with and the vowel in its middle, which is RF.K.3.a and RF.K.3.b beside the phoneme work of RF.K.2.d.

K:vowels-consonants.why: Telling vowel letters from consonant letters does not yet associate long and short sounds with vowel spellings; it is a readiness step.

K:segment-phonemes.why: Segmenting a word into its complete sequence of sounds is exactly RF.1.2.d; RF.K.2.d only isolates the first, middle and last sound of CVC words.

K:cvc-build.why: Found by the reviewer of the first units: RF.K.3 is the heading of its group, not a standard a teacher cites. Building a three-sound word from letters is L.K.2.d (spell simple words phonetically) and L.K.2.c (write a letter for most consonant and short-vowel sounds), and uses RF.K.3.a (letter-sound correspondences for consonants) and RF.K.3.b (the short vowels).

was.why: Building and completing CVC words from letters is phonetic spelling (encoding); L.K.2.d was missing.

K:digraphs-k.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): sorting pictures under the letter teams sh and ch teaches the digraph spellings themselves, which is the Grade 1 standard RF.1.3.a; in a Kindergarten unit it is shown as a later grade, not as "prepares".

was.why: Kindergarten phonics names no digraphs; hearing sh/ch at the start is initial-sound isolation and a readiness step toward the grade 1 digraph standard.

K:word-sentence-tracing.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): the sight-word page (read the word, trace it, write it) is RF.K.3.c, which the rows left out. RF.K.1.c stays for the sentence pages of the point; the unit lesson hands out one-word pages and names L.K.1.a and RF.K.3.c only.

was.why: The skill explicitly practises spaces between words; the print-concept standard RF.K.1.c was missing.

K:articles.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): a and an is the Grade 1 standard L.1.1.h and the pages teach it outright; in a Kindergarten unit it is shown as a later grade.

1:spell-picture-words.why: RF.1.3 is a decoding (reading) standard; spelling words belongs to the L.1.2 spelling components.

1:syllables-split.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): the lesson teaches that every syllable has a vowel sound, which is RF.1.3.d.

was.why: Clapping and counting syllables is the spoken-syllable standard RF.K.2.b, which was missing.

1:alphabetical-order.why: "L.1" is a whole strand, not a standard; ABC order is not named in Common Core and is the readiness step for using beginning dictionaries and glossaries.

1:articles.why: The exact lettered component for articles (determiners) exists; the general L.1.1 was used.

1:cloze.why: Choosing the word that fits a sentence is using sentence-level context (L.1.4.a), not general grammar (L.1.1).

1:question-words.why: Choosing and matching question words does not yet produce interrogative sentences; L.1.1.j is a later step, not taught here.

1:story-sequencing.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): the child retells the whole story in order, which is RL.1.2. [pages-review en.review.json, RL.K.2 prepares] Putting story pictures in order leads up to retelling but is not retelling; the TEKS page already rates the same lesson as a lead-up. [pages-review en.review.json, RL.1.2 prepares] Ordering the sentences of a story leads up to retelling; the central message or lesson of a story is not addressed.

was.why: Ordering pictures and sentences is not writing a narrative; it is a readiness step toward W.1.3.

1:word-classes.why: L.2.1.e is about choosing between adjectives and adverbs (wrong standard) and L.1.1 is too general; nouns/verbs and adjectives have their own components, and naming word classes leads to L.3.1.a. [pages-review en.review.json, L.K.1.b extends] Sorting words by part of speech in Grade 1 and Grade 2 lessons goes beyond using nouns and verbs in Kindergarten speech and writing.

2:sentence-boundaries.why: The capital-letter standard (L.K.2.a) was missing, and splitting run-together sentences is the readiness step for the run-on standard L.4.1.f. [pages-review en.review.json, L.K.2.a extends] The only lesson is a Grade 2 lesson that also splits run-on sentences; nothing addresses the pronoun I.

2:cursive-writing.why: Common Core handwriting stops at printing all letters; cursive goes beyond that standard on the same line and was left unmapped. [pages-review en.review.json, L.1.1.a removed] A Grade 2 cursive lesson does not address a standard about printing letters, and Common Core has no cursive standard to go beyond.
2:cursive-writing.none: A Grade 2 cursive lesson does not address a standard about printing letters, and Common Core has no cursive standard to go beyond.

2:question-words.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): writing whole questions is producing complete interrogative sentences: L.1.1.j, and L.2.1.f in Grade 2; only the Kindergarten question-word standard was listed.

2:describe-a-picture.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): the second page asks for the child's own short story about the picture, which prepares narrative writing (W.2.3).

was.why: Sentences from starters and a word bank are sentence production, not yet an informative text with a topic, developed points and a conclusion.

2:word-classes.why: The code named nouns, verbs and adjectives but only the noun component was read; L.2.1 is too general, and sorting by word class leads to L.3.1.a. [pages-review en.review.json, L.K.1.b extends] Sorting words by part of speech in Grade 1 and Grade 2 lessons goes beyond using nouns and verbs in Kindergarten speech and writing.

2:plural-nouns.why: L.2.1.b covers only irregular plurals; writing regular and irregular plurals together is the grade 3 standard L.3.1.b.

2:spelling-rules.why: Position-based spellings and ending rules are named word for word in L.3.2.f, which was missing. [pages-review en.review.json, RF.2.3 removed] The only lesson is a spelling lesson already claimed under L.2.2.d; it does not teach decoding, and RF.2.3.a to f are not listed at all.

2:read-cursive.none: Common Core has no standard for reading cursive script; RF.2.3 is about phonics and word analysis, not letter style.
2:read-cursive.why: RF.2.3 was attached only because the word 'read' appears; the skill is script recognition.

2:prefixes.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): un-, dis-, in-, re-, pre- and mis- are L.2.4.b in Grade 2 and L.3.4.b and RF.3.3.a in Grade 3; the lesson sits in a Grade 3 unit and carried only the Grade 2 code.

2:mystery-animal.why: Finding an animal from category and attribute clues is defining by category and key attributes (L.1.5.b), which was missing. [pages-review en.review.json, L.1.5.b prepares] Children read clues to find an animal; they do not define a word by its category and attributes themselves. [pages-review en.review.json, RI.2.1 removed] A who-am-I riddle worksheet is not asking and answering questions about key details of an informational text.

2:animal-fact-file.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): no text is read on either page, so RI.2.1 is not taught; W.2.7 (shared research) holds only when the class checks a fact in a book, so it prepares.

was.why: Gathering facts from a provided source to fill a fact file is exactly W.2.8, which was missing.

2:compare-two-animals.why: RI.2.9 compares two texts on the same topic; comparing the facts of two different animals practises the same-and-different step toward it. In Grade 1 the same page prepares RI.1.9 (basic similarities and differences between two texts on one topic): a lesson of the Grade 1 unit on information texts uses it.

3:cursive-sentences.why: Common Core handwriting stops at printing all letters; cursive sentences go beyond that standard on the same line and were left unmapped. [pages-review en.review.json, L.1.1.a removed] A Grade 2 cursive lesson does not address a standard about printing letters, and Common Core has no cursive standard to go beyond.
3:cursive-sentences.none: A Grade 2 cursive lesson does not address a standard about printing letters, and Common Core has no cursive standard to go beyond.

3:word-fields.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): L.3.5.c is about words for states of mind and degrees of certainty (knew, believed, suspected), not verbs for go and look; the content is L.2.5.b.

was.why: L.3.5.c is about words for states of mind and degrees of certainty; telling apart closely related action verbs (stroll/dash, glance/stare) is L.2.5.b.

3:person-words.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): the lesson is mostly the spelling changes when -er is added (drop the e, double the consonant), which is L.3.2.e.

was.why: Knowing the meaning of a common derivational suffix (-er) is also RF.3.3.a, which was missing.

3:root-words-in-context.why: Found by the reviewer of the English literacy units (an American K-3 teacher): choosing among bake, baker, baking and baked is choosing the grammatical form a sentence needs (L.3.1.a, L.3.1.e); L.3.4.c is using a root to work out an unknown word, which the page only reaches toward.

K:human-body.why: "K-LS1" is a whole strand and its one kindergarten standard is about survival needs; naming external body parts is a readiness step for the grade 1 external-parts standard.

K:living-nonliving.why: Telling living from non-living things is a readiness step; K-LS1-1 asks what living things need to survive.

K:fruit-vegetable.why: "K-LS1" is a whole strand; sorting foods into categories is L.K.5.a, and which plant part we eat prepares the grade 1 plant-parts standard.

K:seasons.why: The yearly cycle of seasons leads to the seasonal-pattern standards 1-ESS1-2 and 3-ESS2-1, which were missing.

K:natural-made.why: "K-2-ETS" is a whole strand and engineering design is not this skill; it is a category sort and a readiness step for classifying materials.

K:five-senses.why: "K-LS1" is a whole strand; the senses and their body parts prepare the grade 1 external-parts standard and the grade 4 senses standard.

K:plant-needs.why: That plants need water and light is investigated in 2-LS2-1, which was missing.

K:sink-float.why: "K-PS" is a whole strand and kindergarten physical science is pushes, pulls and sunlight; sink or float is a readiness step for classifying materials by observable properties.

1:animal-classes-coverings.why: 1-LS3-1 is about young resembling their parents (wrong standard); body coverings are external structures, which leads to 4-LS1-1.

1:life-cycles.why: Life cycles are the grade 3 standard 3-LS1-1; ordering stages does not itself compare young with their parents, so 1-LS3-1 is only prepared.

1:sink-float.why: Predicting and testing sink or float is investigating and classifying by observable properties (2-PS1-1); nothing is chosen for an intended purpose, so 2-PS1-2 is only prepared.

1:body-parts.why: Left unmapped, but naming external body parts is the readiness step for the grade 1 external-parts standard (same as K:human-body).

1:five-senses.why: The senses are asked for by name in 4-LS1-2, which was missing.

1:plant-parts.why: What each plant part does leads to the structure-and-function standard 4-LS1-1, which was missing.

2:materials.why: The grouping is done for recycling, so the reduce-human-impact standard K-ESS3-3 was missing.

2:plant-parts.why: What each plant part does leads to the structure-and-function standard 4-LS1-1, which was missing.

2:day-and-night.why: 1-ESS1-1 only observes the pattern; explaining day and night by Earth turning goes beyond it and prepares 5-ESS1-2.

2:habitats-adaptations.why: Naming a helpful body feature is a readiness step for the grade 3 argument about survival in a habitat, not that argument itself.

2:sink-float.why: The clay-boat task shows how the shape of an object helps it function, which is K-2-ETS1-2 and was missing.

3:water-cycle.why: "2-ESS2" is a whole strand; the exact grade 2 standard is 2-ESS2-3, which the water cycle goes beyond, and naming stages only prepares the grade 5 Earth-systems model.

3:planets.none: No K-5 NGSS performance expectation asks for the order or kinds of planets; the solar system is a middle-school topic, and grade 5 Earth-and-space standards are about star brightness and shadow/day-night patterns.
3:planets.why: "5-ESS1" is a whole strand, and neither of its two standards is about the planets.

3:investigation.why: Left unmapped although 3-5-ETS1-3 asks for planning and carrying out fair tests; the sink-or-float content goes beyond the grade 2 investigation standard.

K:transport-flying.why: Sorting pictures into land, water and air transport (and things that fly) is the category sort L.K.5.a asks for; knowing the ways people and goods travel prepares D2.Geo.7 (K-2), which asks why and how they move from place to place.

1:food-groups.why: Sorting foods into the four food groups is the category sort L.1.5.a asks for; knowing the groups prepares identifying the practice of eating from every group (NHES 7.2.1, PreK-2), which the page does not ask.

K:grid-copy.none: Grid copying is a visual-spatial readiness skill; "K.G" is a mathematics strand and no ELA or NGSS standard asks for it.
K:grid-copy.why: It was mapped to a math strand that is not part of these two documents.

2:find-differences.why: One sentence per difference is sentence production, not an informative text with a topic and conclusion; the visual part has no standard.

1:true-false-equations.why: The Grade 1 lesson True or False? hands out the page of that name: the children decide whether equations are true or false, which is 1.OA.D.7 itself. (The earlier "extends" was written when the only lesson on the point was a Grade 3 lesson.)

2:line-plots.why: [pages-review en.review.json, 2.MD.D.9 prepares] Children only read a finished line plot; they do not measure objects or make the plot, which is what the code asks.

3:line-plot-halves.why: [pages-review en.review.json, 3.MD.B.4 prepares] Children only read a line plot marked in halves; they do not measure with a ruler or make the plot.

K:story-sequencing.why: [pages-review en.review.json, RL.K.2 prepares] Putting story pictures in order leads up to retelling but is not retelling; the TEKS page already rates the same lesson as a lead-up.

K:compare-groups.why: The page Color the Greater Number compares two written numerals from 1 to 10, which is K.CC.C.7; the pages with two groups are K.CC.C.6.

1:word-problems.why: Level 1 of the addition and subtraction story pages stays within 10 with a picture of the objects: the Kindergarten standard K.OA.A.2. The year design places those pages in Kindergarten.

2:bundle-ten-ones.why: More Than Nine of a Kind, level 1, shows more than nine ten-rods to trade for a hundred: 2.NBT.A.1.a (100 as a bundle of ten tens).

3:column-regrouping.why: Adding and subtracting three-digit numbers in columns with a new ten or hundred is taught in Grade 2 (2.NBT.B.7: within 1000 with strategies based on place value, related to a written method) and made fluent in Grade 3.

2:equal-shares-shapes.why: Deciding whether a circle or rectangle is cut into equal shares, and naming halves and fourths, is 1.G.A.3; thirds and the Grade 2 wording are 2.G.A.3.

1:hundreds-chart.why: Level 1 of The Hundreds Chart shows the numbers 1 to 100 with eight boxes to fill: counting to 100 by ones, K.CC.A.1. The year design places that page in Kindergarten, near the hundredth day of school.

2:add-with-blocks.why: Level 2 of Add the Blocks adds two two-digit numbers shown as rods and cubes with no new ten and a sum up to 99: 1.NBT.C.4 (adding within 100 with concrete models, tens with tens and ones with ones).

1:near-doubles.why: Found by the reviewer of the Grade 2 unit Fact Strategies Within 20 (an American Grade 2 teacher, 2026-11-13): doubles from memory and the near doubles built on them are mental strategies of 2.OA.B.2 ("fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies"); the Grade 1 lesson prepares it, the Grade 2 lesson teaches it. The row from the point's own code stays.

3:area-model.why: The point holds three kinds of page: rectangles tiled with unit squares (7.a), rectangles with two side lengths to multiply (7.b: Area of a Rectangle: Multiply the Side Lengths), and L-shapes cut into two rectangles whose areas are added (7.d: Area of an L-Shape). Each lesson of a unit shows the one it teaches.

2:subtract-with-blocks.why: The point carries 2.NBT.B.7 for its page with base-ten blocks (Take Away the Blocks). Subtract and Open a Ten: Tens-and-Ones Mat subtracts a one- or two-digit number from a two-digit number in a drawing of sticks and dots: within 100, with a strategy based on place value (2.NBT.B.5).

2:column-method.why: The column pages add and subtract two two-digit numbers (2.NBT.B.5) and two three-digit numbers (2.NBT.B.7). Add Three and Four Two-Digit Numbers adds three or four two-digit numbers in columns: 2.NBT.B.6. Each lesson of a unit shows the one it teaches.

3:times-tables.why: The point carries 3.OA.C.7 for its pages on the multiplication facts. Multiply by Tens multiplies a one-digit number by a multiple of ten from 20 to 90 with the facts and place value (4 × 6 tens = 24 tens = 240): 3.NBT.A.3. Each lesson of a unit shows the one it teaches.

1:measure-length-units.why: The point carries 1.MD.A.1 and 1.MD.A.2 for its pages on ordering lengths and measuring with units laid end to end. Same Length, Two Units measures one ribbon with paper clips and with cubes and asks which unit was needed more often: measuring twice with units of different lengths and relating the two numbers to the size of the unit is 2.MD.A.2. Each lesson of a unit shows the one it teaches.

2:compare-lengths.why: The point carries 2.MD.A.4 for its page on measuring two objects and finding how much longer one is. Length Story Problems tells lengths in one unit that are put together, cut off and compared, with a bar model and an equation: word problems within 100 about lengths are 2.MD.B.5. Each lesson of a unit shows the one it teaches.

K:birds-eye-view.why: Matching a thing seen from the side to the same thing seen from above (and a room drawn from above) is the overhead view every map is made of; the child neither constructs a map nor uses one to describe a place, so the page prepares D2.Geo.1 and D2.Geo.2 (K-2).

K:family.none: The C3 Framework names no family members, kinship words or family tree in its K-2 indicators (civics, economics, geography, history).
K:family.why: Family members and family words on a tree are family vocabulary; no K-2 indicator of the four disciplines asks for them, and forcing a history or civics code would misstate the page.

K:wants-needs.why: Telling a need from a want is the step before D2.Eco.1 (K-2), which asks how scarcity makes people decide; the page sorts, it does not yet weigh a choice.

K:community-helpers.why: Matching each helper to a tool names the work people do for a community; D2.Civ.2 (K-2) asks the child to explain how all people play important roles in it, which the page leads up to but does not ask.

1:map-key.why: Finding each key symbol on the map, counting it and following steps on a map use a map to describe a place (D2.Geo.2, K-2); the page where the child draws a map with its own key constructs one (D2.Geo.1, K-2).

1:family-generations.why: Putting family words in order from the oldest generation to the youngest orders people in time, the step before the chronological sequence of events D2.His.1 (K-2) asks for; no K-2 indicator names a family tree.

2:cardinal-directions.why: Labeling north, east, south and west and using them to say which picture lies which way on a map is using a map to describe places and how they relate to each other (D2.Geo.2, K-2).

2:continents.why: Labeling the continents on a world map is the map knowledge D2.Geo.3 (K-2) builds on; the indicator asks for the cultural and environmental characteristics of places, which the page does not.

2:family-relationships.none: The C3 Framework names no family relationships in its K-2 indicators (civics, economics, geography, history).
2:family-relationships.why: Naming an aunt or a cousin from a riddle is family vocabulary; no K-2 indicator of the four disciplines asks for it.

3:continents-oceans.why: Locating the continents and oceans on a world map is where D2.Geo.2 (3-5) starts; the indicator goes on to explain how those locations relate to environmental characteristics, which the page does not ask.

K:healthy-food.why: Sorting foods into everyday and sometimes foods identifies a practice that supports health (NHES 7.2.1, PreK-2) and gives the child what NHES 5.2.4 asks next: choosing the option that supports health.

K:hygiene-habits.why: Matching each body-care job to its tool and putting the hand-washing steps in order identify practices that support health (NHES 7.2.1) and a way to prevent illness (NHES 1.2.3), PreK-2.

K:road-safety.why: Reading the traffic light and putting stop, look, listen, cross in order identify a way to prevent injury (NHES 1.2.3) and a safe practice (NHES 7.2.1), PreK-2; obeying the light is a rule outside school whose purpose D2.Civ.3 (K-2) asks the child to explain.

1:healthy-habits.why: Brushing at the right moments and choosing the way that stops germs identify healthy practices (NHES 7.2.1) and ways to prevent illness (NHES 1.2.3); checking off the habits done each day is the first step to taking action on a health goal (NHES 6.2.5), PreK-2.

1:road-signs.why: Knowing what each road sign means identifies ways to prevent injury (NHES 1.2.3, PreK-2); a sign is a rule outside school, and explaining why it exists (D2.Civ.3, K-2) is the step after matching it to its meaning.

2:healthy-habits-why.why: Matching each habit (washing hands, brushing teeth, sleep, moving, sun protection) to the reason we do it describes health-promoting behaviors (NHES 1.2.4) and the illnesses and injuries they prevent (NHES 1.2.3), PreK-2.

2:road-signs.why: Choosing the sign that fits a situation identifies ways to prevent injury on the road (NHES 1.2.3, PreK-2); sorting signs by what they are for (warning, must-not, information) leads up to explaining the purposes of rules outside school (D2.Civ.3, K-2), which the page does not ask.

K:feelings.why: Naming how I feel and matching faces to feeling words is expressing feelings, which NHES 4.2.1 (PreK-2) asks for; the C3 Framework holds no social-emotional indicator.

K:i-can.why: Drawing what I am good at and what I am learning, and circling who helps me, identifies strengths and assets that support health and well-being (NHES 1.2.1, PreK-2).

K:sleep-play.why: Ordering bath, pajamas and bed and circling the ways to play that move the whole body tell why sleep and play matter for health (NHES 1.2.5, PreK-2) and lead to practicing those behaviors (NHES 7.2.1).

K:trusted-adults.why: Circling the grown-ups who could help (a police officer, a firefighter, a doctor, a nurse, a teacher) among children, and the rule to check first with one's own grown-up, identify characteristics of trusted adults (NHES 3.2.1, PreK-2).

K:calm-down.why: Saying "I need a break, please." or "Can you help me?" makes a request that supports health and well-being (NHES 8.2.1, PreK-2); naming the feeling first leads to expressing feelings and needs (NHES 4.2.1).

K:kind-words.why: Circling the kind act in each scene (helping up, building together, sharing) and tracing kind words demonstrate ways to show kindness and compassion (NHES 4.2.5, PreK-2).

K:space-bubble.why: Asking "May I give you a hug?", accepting either answer and stopping at "Stop, please." communicate and respect the boundaries of self and others (NHES 4.2.4, PreK-2).

K:germ-busters.why: Choosing the times to wash and washing for two "Happy Birthday" songs demonstrate practices that support the health of self and others (NHES 7.2.2) and identify a healthy practice (NHES 7.2.1), PreK-2.

1:ask-a-grown-up.why: Telling the things only a trusted grown-up gives or uses and asking first is recognizing when help is needed for a health-related decision (NHES 5.2.2, PreK-2).

1:myplate-groups.why: Sorting foods into the five MyPlate groups identifies practices that support health (NHES 7.2.1, PreK-2).

1:myplate-lunch.why: Building a MyPlate lunch and finding the times of the day a food or drink is chosen identify when a health-related decision is needed (NHES 5.2.1, PreK-2).

1:habit-to-grow.why: Checking the habits a child does and choosing one to grow determines a health behavior to change or reinforce (NHES 6.2.1, PreK-2).

1:health-helpers.why: Naming the school nurse and the town health helpers locates school and community health helpers (NHES 3.2.3, PreK-2).

1:whole-body-listening.why: Whole-body listening (eyes on the speaker, quiet hands and feet, a calm body) is an active listening skill (NHES 4.2.2, PreK-2).

1:fire-safety-911.why: Getting out, crawling low, stop-drop-roll and calling 911 when someone needs help demonstrate when and how to seek help (NHES 3.2.2, PreK-2).

1:say-no-go-tell.why: Saying no, going away and telling a trusted adult are communication skills to use when uncomfortable or unsafe (NHES 4.2.3, PreK-2).

1:help-a-friend.why: Friendly reminders and invitations to play are ways to support others in making health-promoting choices (NHES 8.2.2, PreK-2).

2:three-ways-healthy.why: Sorting healthy actions into body, feelings and friendships identifies dimensions of wellness (NHES 1.2.2, PreK-2).

2:who-helps-me-choose.why: Naming the family, friends, media and other things that shape a choice identifies influences on health (NHES 2.2.1, PreK-2).

2:ad-detective.why: Finding what an ad wants and how it tries to persuade determines how an influence affects health (NHES 2.2.2, PreK-2).

2:health-goal.why: Choosing a health goal and someone to help identifies a goal that supports health (NHES 6.2.2, PreK-2).

2:nurse-doctor-dentist.why: Telling when to see the nurse, the doctor or the dentist explains when it is important to seek health care (NHES 1.2.7, PreK-2).

2:how-did-my-goal-go.why: Looking back on a goal, what helped and what to try next, reflects on the results of goal-setting (NHES 6.2.6, PreK-2).

2:stop-think-choose.why: Stopping to think about the choices and what could happen describes options and outcomes for a health decision (NHES 5.2.3, PreK-2).

2:sun-heat-cold.why: Getting ready for sun, heat and cold identifies how the environment affects health (NHES 1.2.6, PreK-2).

2:health-poster.why: A class poster for a healthy choice encourages others to make health-promoting choices (NHES 8.2.3, PreK-2).

3:how-germs-spread.why: Explaining how germs spread and how washing, covering a cough and using your own cup stop them explains ways to prevent illness (NHES 1.5.3, grades 3-5).

3:myplate-day.why: Planning a day of meals with all five food groups and choosing water or milk chooses a health-promoting option (NHES 5.5.4, grades 3-5).

3:sleep-screens-play.why: Looking at the hours of sleep, screens and active play in a day examines practices that support health (NHES 7.5.1, grades 3-5).

3:what-sways-my-choices.why: Working out how family, friends, ads and videos sway a choice determines how influences affect the health of self and others (NHES 2.5.2, grades 3-5).

3:goal-plan-track.why: A goal plan with steps, things needed, helpers and a tracking chart develops a plan with actions, resources and progress-tracking (NHES 6.5.3, grades 3-5).

3:fire-escape-plan.why: Drawing and practising a home escape plan demonstrates a practice that supports the safety of self and others (NHES 7.5.2, grades 3-5).

3:who-can-help.why: Matching each situation to the right trusted adult or resource determines which helpers are appropriate in various situations (NHES 3.5.1, grades 3-5).

3:big-feelings.why: Naming a feeling, calming down and saying what you feel and need uses communication skills to express feelings and needs (NHES 4.5.1, grades 3-5).

3:solve-a-conflict.why: Calming down, telling each side and finding a fair solution demonstrates strategies to resolve conflict (NHES 4.5.6, grades 3-5).

3:say-no-walk-away.why: Saying no clearly, giving a reason and walking away demonstrates refusal skills (NHES 4.5.5, grades 3-5).

K:class-rules.why: Choosing, in each pair of the same moment, the picture that follows a class rule (walking in the hall, raising a hand, cleaning up, listening at story time) identifies how rules work in the classroom and school (D2.Civ.12, K-2); saying which picture keeps everyone safe or helps us learn leads up to the purposes of rules (D2.Civ.3, K-2).

K:take-turns-share.why: Telling friends who take turns, share and help from acts that are not kind (grabbing, pushing, knocking down a tower), and drawing myself helping a friend, apply civic virtues in school settings (D2.Civ.7, K-2).

K:many-kinds-of-families.why: Seeing six kinds of family (one parent, two fathers, a grandmother raising grandchildren, a foster family, a big family) and drawing the people who care for me name the family as the first group whose members share tasks and care; D2.Civ.6 (K-2) asks how communities accomplish common tasks and fill roles, which the page leads up to but does not ask.

K:family-traditions.why: Matching each tradition's object (a party hat, a pie, a diya, a red envelope) to the family scene that keeps it, and drawing my own family's tradition, identify cultural practices; D2.Geo.6 (K-2) ties cultural characteristics to specific places, which the page does not ask.

K:long-ago-today.why: Matching each long-ago thing (a washboard and tub, a candle, a horse and buggy, a wall telephone) to the thing that does the same job today compares life in the past to life today (D2.His.2, K-2).

K:choosing-one-thing.why: With one coin, one recess or one library book, the child chooses one thing and crosses out the one given up: the limit makes the decision (D2.Eco.1, K-2), and the choice and the thing given up are its benefit and its cost (D2.Eco.2, K-2).

K:goods-and-services.why: Matching each worker (a baker, a builder, a barber, a mail carrier) to the good they make or the service they do names goods and services and who produces them; D2.Eco.3 (K-2) asks for the skills and knowledge each job needs, which the lesson only begins ("what did each worker have to learn?").

K:our-flag.why: Coloring the flag of the United States and counting its 13 stripes name the country and its symbol; D2.Civ.5 (K-2) asks what governments are and what they do, which the lesson only begins (leaders who make rules for the whole country).

K:martin-luther-king.why: The true story of Martin Luther King Jr., who worked peacefully with many others to change laws that kept Black people and white people apart, describes how people have tried to improve their communities (D2.Civ.14, K-2); drawing children playing a fair game leads up to fairness and equality (D2.Civ.8, K-2).

K:fair-for-everyone.why: Choosing, in each pair of the same moment, the one that is fair to everyone (taking turns on the swing, crackers shared, everyone in the game) and drawing how to make an unfair moment fair describe fairness and equality (D2.Civ.8, K-2).

K:land-and-water.why: Coloring the water and the land of a globe that shows North and South America, and finding the United States on the class globe, use a globe to identify environmental characteristics of places (D2.Geo.3, K-2).

K:neighborhood-map.why: Finding the school and the park on a map with a picture key and drawing a path along the streets from a house to the school use a map to describe places and how they connect (D2.Geo.2, K-2); drawing my own house and a path onto the map leads up to constructing a map (D2.Geo.1, K-2).

K:hot-cold-places.why: Sending each thing (a coat, mittens, a sled, a swimsuit, sandals, a beach ball) to the snowy town or the beach town where people use it explains how weather and climate affect people's lives in a place (D2.Geo.4, K-2).

K:school-helpers.why: After a school walk on which each adult says what they are in charge of, matching each problem (a hurt knee, a spill, a book to find, an empty lunch tray, going home early) to the school helper who handles it describes the roles and responsibilities of people in authority at school (D2.Civ.1, K-2), and leads up to how all people play important roles in a community (D2.Civ.2, K-2).

K:class-vote.why: Voting once, counting the votes together on a class graph and reading the book that won, even when my own book did not win, show how people work together to make decisions in the classroom (D2.Civ.11, K-2).
